Series::float_power¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series Series::float_power(const Series& other) const
Series Series::float_power(double other) const
Series& Series::float_power_(const Series& other)

What It Does¶

Raises each element to a power, always in floating point:

float_power(a, b) = a ** b

The one difference from pow() is dtype. pow() follows the usual type-promotion rules — two integer operands give an integer result. float_power() promotes both operands to float64 first (or complex128 if either side is complex) and returns that. Use it when you want a real-valued power regardless of how the inputs are typed — fractional exponents, 2 ** -1, or just guarding against a surprise integer truncation.

Parameters¶

other (const Series& or double): the exponent b. A Series broadcasts against the receiver; a double applies the same exponent everywhere.

Returns¶

Series or Series& a ** b as float64 (or complex128 for complex inputs). Because an in-place call cannot change dtype, float_power_() requires a Float64 or Complex128 receiver and a Series exponent.

Gradient¶

float_power() is differentiable, with the same rules as pow() evaluated in double precision:

d/da (a ** b) = b * a ** (b - 1)
d/db (a ** b) = a ** b * ln(a)

Examples¶

Example 1. Integer operands still produce a float64 result.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({2, 3, 4}).float_power(pluss::make_series({3, 2, 0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[8.0000, 9.0000, 1.0000]

The same call through pow() would return an integer series.

Example 2. Fractional and large exponents.

pluss::series::print(
    std::cout,
    pluss::make_series({4.0, 9.0, 2.0})
        .float_power(pluss::make_series({0.5, 0.5, 10.0})));

Output¶

Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[2.0000, 3.0000, 1024.0000]

Example 3. A scalar exponent.

pluss::series::print(std::cout, pluss::make_series({2, 3}).float_power(2.0));

Output¶

Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[4.0000, 9.0000]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • The result dtype is always float64 (or complex128), never float32 and never integer — even when both inputs are float32. Cast down with to() if you need float32.

  • A negative base with a non-integer exponent gives NaN on the real path, just as with pow().

  • For integer-preserving exponentiation, use pow() instead.

  • float_power_() cannot promote an integer or Float32 receiver. Use the out-of-place result when promotion is required.

Summary¶

float_power(a, b) is a ** b forced into floating point:

  • both operands promote to float64 (complex128 if complex); result matches

  • differentiable, with the pow() rules in double precision

  • float_power_() is the in-place form

See Also¶

  • Series::pow: exponentiation with ordinary type promotion.

  • Series::exp2 / Series::ldexp: the base-2 special cases.

  • Series::sqrt: float_power(x, 0.5).
